content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
Start here: is someone forwarding your calls?

This is the one from the video, and it is the single most important check. Open your phone dialer and enter the master interrogation code below, then hit call. Your carrier answers with the status of every forwarding rule on your line. You want every line to read Disabled . If it shows On and a phone number you do not recognize, every call and text to you is being silently copied to that number, and the person on the other end sees it all.

If it comes back clean, you are good. If it does not, jump to the wipe code in the next block, then the response playbook near the bottom.

*#21#

The one-shot wipe (nuke every forwarding rule)

If the master check showed forwarding you did not set up, this erases all call-forwarding rules on your SIM in one move, no menus, no per-rule digging. Enter it, hit call, wait for the 'erased' confirmations, then run *#21# again to confirm everything reads Disabled.

Harmless to run even if you are clean, it just resets forwarding to off.

##002#

Your phone's fingerprint (IMEI)

Every phone has a unique IMEI, its serial number on the cellular network. You need it to report a phone stolen, to check a used phone against a blacklist before buying, or to unlock it. This code shows yours instantly and works on literally every phone, iPhone or Android, any carrier.

*#06#

How the attack actually works (so you can spot it)

Knowing the attacker's move is how you recognize it on your own device. Unconditional call forwarding is set with a code shaped like **21* followed by a number and a # . Someone with 60 seconds of physical access to an unlocked phone types it in, and from that moment every call rings on their phone too. There is no notification, no icon, nothing.

That is exactly why *#21# exists as the counter-check, and ##002# as the undo. Only ever run forwarding codes on a phone you own. Setting forwarding on someone else's line without permission is illegal, this section is here so you can catch it being done to you, not do it to anyone.

Every iPhone / GSM code

These work on any GSM line (AT&T, T-Mobile, most of the world). A few behave differently or not at all on Verizon's older CDMA network, see the carrier section for that.

SIM security codes

These manage the PIN on the physical SIM itself, the layer that stops someone popping your SIM into another phone. Handle with care, too many wrong PUK entries can permanently lock the SIM.

Your PUK is printed on the plastic card the SIM came in, or in your carrier account. If you lose it, your carrier can reissue it.

Android secret codes (dedicated section)

Android has its own layer of hidden codes, most in the *#*#...#*#* shape, that open engineering and test menus. Two big caveats: many are manufacturer-specific (these lean Samsung), and Google has disabled a lot of them on newer Android for security, so not every code fires on every phone. The GSM call-forwarding codes above ( *#21# , ##002# ) also work on any Android GSM line.

Treat the last two like live wires, *2767*3855# starts wiping the instant you press call, with no 'are you sure'.

Codes by carrier

Two things change by carrier: the exact strings for forwarding and account info, and whether GSM MMI codes work at all. Verizon grew up on CDMA, so the umbrella *#21# interrogation historically did not work there, you use the *72 / *73 vertical codes instead. AT&T and T-Mobile are GSM, so the codes above work as written.

Universal star codes (any US line)

These are vertical service codes, they work on essentially every US carrier and even landlines, no # needed. Dial the code right before the number where noted.

Troubleshooting (why the errors happen)

"Setting interrogation failed" on *#21# . The network could not read that forwarding condition. Usual causes: you are on a CDMA carrier (Verizon, old Sprint) that does not fully support GSM interrogation, Wi-Fi Calling intercepted the code, you are on a dual-SIM / eSIM phone and queried the wrong line, or one forwarding type (fax / data) simply is not provisioned. Fix: turn Wi-Fi Calling off, make sure you have real cellular signal, pick the right SIM line in Settings, then retry. Or check the conditions one at a time with *#61# , *#62# , *#67# instead of the umbrella *#21# .

"Connection problem or invalid MMI code." The string was mistyped, your carrier does not support that MMI, you are on CDMA, or Wi-Fi Calling swallowed it. Fix: retype it exactly (it is picky), turn off Wi-Fi Calling, confirm cellular signal, or use the carrier-specific star codes above.

Codes do nothing on Verizon. CDMA heritage, use the *72 / *73 style codes in the carrier table.

Field Test numbers look negative. dBm signal is negative, and closer to zero is stronger, -80 dBm is a great signal, -110 dBm is nearly no bars.

Dual SIM confusion. MMI codes only query the currently selected line, switch your default line in Settings if the results look wrong.

If someone IS forwarding your calls (response playbook)

You ran *#21# and it showed forwarding to a number you do not know. Do this in order:

- Run ##002# to wipe every forwarding rule, then *#21# again to confirm it all reads Disabled.

- Change your SIM PIN with **04* , so your SIM cannot be moved to another phone.

- Change your Apple ID / Google account password and turn on two-factor, forwarding is often the tip of a bigger access problem.

- Check Settings for Wi-Fi Calling and any unfamiliar call-forwarding entries in Phone settings.

- If it keeps coming back, someone has ongoing access, factory reset the phone and call your carrier to reissue the SIM.

Use this responsibly

Everything here is for checking and securing your own phone, or one you have explicit permission to test. The interrogation and wipe codes are safe on your own line. The forwarding-setup codes are not a toy, configuring forwarding or barring on someone else's phone without consent is illegal in most places. Save this, run the master check on your own phone, and send it to someone you care about so they can too.

Frequently asked questions

It interrogates your carrier for all call-forwarding rules on your line, voice, data, SMS, fax. If any read 'On' with a number you did not set, your calls and texts are being copied to that number. You want every line to say Disabled.

Yes. It simply erases every call-forwarding rule on your SIM and resets forwarding to off. If you had none set up, nothing changes. If spyware forwarding was set, it wipes it. Run *#21# afterward to confirm.

The network could not read one of the forwarding conditions, usually because you are on a CDMA carrier like Verizon, Wi-Fi Calling intercepted the code, or you queried the wrong SIM on a dual-SIM phone. Turn off Wi-Fi Calling, confirm cellular signal, and retry, or check conditions individually with *#61# , *#62# , *#67# .

The GSM call-forwarding codes ( *#21# , ##002# , *#06# ) work on any Android GSM line. Android also has its own *#*#...#*#* engineering codes, see the dedicated Android section, though many are manufacturer-specific and some are disabled on newer phones.

Verizon grew up on CDMA, which does not support the GSM MMI interrogation codes the same way. Use the vertical codes instead, *72 + number to forward, *73 to cancel, #225 for balance. See the carrier table.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
The two things that stop everyone

The confirmation email. Almost every data broker sends a verification link after you submit an opt-out, and the removal does not happen until someone clicks it. That is where people quit, halfway through, with forty unconfirmed requests sitting in an inbox.

Removal is temporary. Brokers rebuild their listings from public records, so you reappear within weeks and nobody goes back to check.

ChatGPT Work closes both. The Gmail connector lets it find the confirmation emails and click them itself, and scheduled tasks let it re-run the entire sweep without being asked again.

Before you start

A paid ChatGPT plan. Work is bundled into Plus at no extra cost, so if you already pay for ChatGPT you have it.

The web version is fine. The agent browser runs on the web version, so you do not need the desktop app to do any of this. It opens the sites and fills in the forms either way.

You do not need to tell it who you are. It already has your name from your account, which is why the prompts are shorter than you would expect. If it asks for a city or an age to separate you from someone with the same name, give it then.

Prompt 1: Find every site holding your data

This one builds the map. It sends the agent browser across the people-search sites and brokers rather than skimming the first page of Google, and the table it returns is what everything else works from.

Expect the results to be worse than you think they will be.

Search the internet for everything you can find about me. Use your agent browser and go through the people search sites and data brokers, not just the first page of Google. For every site that has my personal information, give me the site name, exactly what it is exposing about me, and the exact opt-out link. Put it all in one table.

Connect Gmail before the next prompt

Do this now, before you run the opt-out prompt, because the next step depends on it.

Press the + button in the message box and select Gmail . That is what lets ChatGPT open the confirmation emails and click the verification links itself.

If it will not connect, restart the session and try again. That clears it almost every time.

Prompt 2: Opt out everywhere, and confirm it

This is the one that matters. The first half submits the removals. The second half is the part that was impossible before the Gmail connector, and it is the difference between a request and an actual removal.

Verification links expire, usually in 24 to 72 hours. An unconfirmed request quietly dies.

The last line is worth keeping. A few brokers ask for a photo ID, and that is a decision you want to make yourself.

Work through that table one site at a time. Open each opt-out page, fill in my details, and submit the removal request. Then check my Gmail for the confirmation emails those sites send back, open each one, and click the verification link inside it. Keep a running log of what has been submitted, what has been confirmed, and anything that failed. Stop and ask me before uploading any ID or making a decision on my behalf.

Prompt 3: Keep yourself erased

Removal does not hold. Brokers rebuild from public records, and a name that was clean in March is usually back by May. The scheduled task is what makes it stick, because the re-check happens whether or not you remember.

45 days is the sweet spot. It lines up with how fast most brokers relist, without burying you in reports.

Create a scheduled task that runs this entire process every 45 days. Each time, re-check the same sites for any new listing of me, submit the opt-out again for anything that has come back, click the new confirmation emails in my Gmail, and send me a short summary of what it found and what it removed.

What it cannot do

Worth knowing so you are not surprised halfway through.

Some brokers require photo ID. A handful will not process a removal without a government ID upload. That is your call to make, not something to hand to an agent, which is why the stop-and-ask line is in prompt 2.

Court records and public filings stay. Property records, court documents and business filings are public by law. You can remove the broker's copy, not the source.

Google results are separate. Taking the listing down does not clear the search result. Use Results about you for that side.

It will not be perfect. Expect the big brokers gone, a long tail that needs a second pass, and a few that need you personally.

Why you are on these sites at all

You never signed up for any of them. Data brokers assemble profiles from public records, loyalty programs, app permissions, warranty cards and each other, then sell the result. Being listed is the default, not something you opted into, which is why the removal burden lands on you.

To see the scale of it first, see exactly what the internet already knows about you . To run the same thing on Claude, the Claude version is here .

Frequently asked questions

Restart the session and try again. Press the plus button in the message box, select Gmail, and reconnect. That clears it almost every time.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
What happened when I raced them

I gave ChatGPT and Claude the same prompt: using your Chrome extension, create 15 meetings on my Google Calendar. Two browsers side by side. ChatGPT was slow on the first meeting, then it figured out the pattern and blazed through the rest. Claude kept hitting page errors, got stuck around meeting 8, and had 12 of 15 on the calendar when ChatGPT was already done.

The part that matters for you: the extension works inside the Chrome you're already logged into. No API keys. No connectors to wire up. It opens the tab, clicks the buttons, and asks you before it touches a new site. Now here's the setup.

Step 1. Get the ChatGPT desktop app

The Chrome plugin is switched on from the desktop app, so you need that first. Download it from openai.com/chatgpt/download for Mac or Windows and sign in with your normal ChatGPT account.

If you already have it, update it first. The Plugins tab only shows on the current version.

Step 2. Turn on the Chrome plugin

Open the desktop app and look at the left sidebar. Click Plugins . Search for Chrome . The card says Control Chrome with ChatGPT. Open it and scroll to the bottom, there's a setup link that takes you to the ChatGPT extension on the Chrome Web Store . Add it to Chrome, approve the permission prompts, and pin it next to your address bar.

One catch. It has to be real Google Chrome. Chromium browsers like Brave or Edge won't work with the plugin yet.

Boom, that's the whole install. Back in the desktop app the Chrome plugin shows as connected, and in Chrome you get a ChatGPT side chat on any tab.

Step 3. Give it the first job

In the desktop app, start a new chat and type @Chrome before the task. That tells ChatGPT to use the extension instead of its own cloud browser. The first time it opens a site it asks for permission, click Allow and stay at your computer, it pauses for you on anything sensitive.

This is the exact prompt from my race. Change the date and it's yours.

@Chrome Create 15 meetings on my Google Calendar for [date]. Each one is 30 minutes, back to back starting at 8:00 AM, titled Meeting 1 through Meeting 15, no guests. Use the calendar tab that's already open. Tell me when all 15 are saved.

Step 4. Turn on Computer Use (it runs your other apps too)

The Chrome plugin only drives the browser. Computer Use is the bigger switch: ChatGPT sees your screen and clicks and types inside any desktop app on Mac or Windows. Finder, Excel, CapCut, your DAW, whatever is open.

Turn it on the same way. In the desktop app switch to Work mode (or Codex), open Plugins , find Computer Use and click Install plugin. Flip on both toggles, the server and the skill, then hit Try now . Then go to Settings, Computer use and review which apps it's allowed to touch.

On a Mac it asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, say yes to both or it can't see the app. On Windows it runs in the foreground, so keep the app visible and let it have the mouse while it works.

Now you can type @Computer and name the app. It asks before it uses an app for the first time and before anything sensitive. It won't run your terminal, it won't touch admin prompts, and it can't drive ChatGPT itself. This is my favorite use of it, Computer Use and the Chrome plugin in one prompt:

@Computer Open the folder [path] and find the 5 newest videos. Then in the Chrome tab with Meta Business Suite Planner open, upload them one at a time and schedule each one for 9:00 AM on the next 5 days, oldest video first. Ask me before you save each post.

Apply to 500 jobs with it

This is the one everybody asks for. Open LinkedIn in Chrome, make sure you're logged in with your resume uploaded, then paste this. It runs through the Easy Apply listings and answers the screening questions from the details you give it. Do it in batches of 50 so LinkedIn doesn't flag the account. The resume side of this, the one that gets past the ATS filters, is in the 500 jobs guide .

@Chrome Go to LinkedIn Jobs, search for [job title] in [city or Remote] with the Easy Apply filter on, sorted by most recent. Apply to every Easy Apply job on the first 2 pages using my saved resume. Answer screening questions from these details: [years of experience], [work authorization], [salary range]. If a question needs something I didn't give you, skip that job and note it. Skip any job that requires a cover letter or sends you to an external site. When you're done, give me a list of every job you applied to with links.

Schedule a month of content in one prompt

Put your 30 videos in one folder with a captions.txt next to them, one caption per line in the same order. Because it runs through the desktop app, the extension can reach the files on your computer, so it uploads from your folder and pastes the matching caption. I did my next month in under 2 minutes. Open Meta Business Suite in a tab first and pick the Instagram account.

@Chrome Open Meta Business Suite, Planner, for my Instagram account. Schedule one post per day for the next 30 days at 9:00 AM, using the videos in [folder path] in filename order and the matching line from captions.txt in that folder as the caption. Check each caption matches its video before you save it. Tell me the count when all 30 are scheduled.

Repost your reels to Facebook (this doubled my views)

Your best reels are sitting on Instagram doing nothing for your Facebook page. I took my top 100, dripped them onto the page 3 a day, and my views doubled this month. Two things before you upload. Give each video a quiet ambient audio bed so the audio isn't a straight duplicate of the Instagram upload, and write a fresh caption for a cold audience that has never seen you.

The audio bed is one ffmpeg command per video. The video track is copied, nothing gets re-encoded:

ffmpeg -i reel.mp4 -i ambient.mp3 -filter_complex "[1:a]volume=0.15[bed];[0:a][bed]amix=inputs=2:duration=first:dropout_transition=0[a]" -map 0:v -map "[a]" -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 128k reel_fb.mp4

The Facebook scheduling prompt

Now let the extension do the scheduling through Bulk upload reels on your page's content calendar. Facebook's bulk tool takes about 35 videos at a time, so split a big batch in two.

@Chrome Open my Facebook Page's Professional Dashboard, Content calendar, Create a post, Bulk upload reels. Upload the videos in [folder path] in filename order and paste the matching line from captions.txt as each caption. Schedule 3 per day at 9:00 AM, 2:00 PM and 7:00 PM starting tomorrow. Wait for each video preview to render before moving on. Before you save, check every caption and time against the list. Tell me the count when they're all scheduled.

Keep it on a leash

It acts as you, inside your logged-in accounts, so a few rules. It asks before every new site and every new app, keep that on. In the desktop app, Settings, Computer Use, you can allowlist the sites and apps it's allowed to touch and block the rest. Never hand it a payment form or a password reset. Watch the first run of any new task, then let it go. And go in batches on LinkedIn and Facebook, fast repeated clicking gets rate limited the same way bots do.

For educational purposes. Automating a site you don't own can break its terms, so keep it to your own accounts.

Frequently asked questions

The extension and the desktop app are free downloads. Browser control is rolling out by plan and region, so if the Plugins tab doesn't show Chrome yet, update the app and check again in a few days. It's listed on the Chrome Web Store as ChatGPT, publisher OpenAI. Computer Use is the one that needs ChatGPT Work or Codex.

Yes. The extension on its own gives you the side chat. Controlling the browser is switched on from the desktop app's Plugins tab, Computer Use lives there too, and that's also how it reaches files on your computer for uploads.

The Chrome plugin drives tabs inside Chrome, @Chrome in your prompt. Computer Use sees your whole screen and works inside any desktop app, @Computer plus the app name. Use the plugin for anything that lives on a website, Computer Use for the apps around it.

No. The plugin only drives real Google Chrome right now. Chromium browsers are not supported. Computer Use can still click around any app, including those browsers, it just won't have the plugin's tab access.

It asks before each new site and app, and you can allowlist or block them in Settings, Computer Use. Keep payments and passwords away from it, stay at the computer on the first run, and work in batches so you don't trip the platform's spam limits. 1. The Bill and Contract Auditor

Most people sign things they never read and pay charges they never question. This flips that. Paste the document and Claude lists every charge and clause working against you, ranked by what each one costs you, with a read on whether it is even enforceable. Two rules. Redact account numbers, reference numbers, and anything personal before you paste, the audit works exactly the same without them. And treat the enforceability calls as a starting point for your own pushback, not legal advice. Verify before you dispute anything.

Read this bill/contract: [paste]. List every charge or clause overcharging me or not in my favor, ranked by cost, and whether each is even enforceable.

2. Voice Note → Email, In Your Voice

The gap between how you talk and how you write is where most emails die. Record yourself talking it out, grab the transcript from your phone's voice memos or just dictate straight into your notes app, then paste it with a sample of your real writing. The sample is the step everyone skips, and it is the whole trick. Without it you get generic AI email. With it you get your voice, minus the rambling.

Here's a transcript of me rambling: [paste]. Rewrite it as a clear [email/post] in a natural first-person voice. Match how I write using this sample: [paste sample].

3. Idea → Working App

One sentence in, working code out, plus run instructions written for someone who has never touched a terminal. Claude even previews the app right in the chat, so you can click around before you save a single file. Be honest about the scope. This builds a single-page tool, a calculator, a tracker, a converter. It is not a startup in a prompt. But the little app you have been meaning to build for a year? It ships today, free.

Build me a working single-page web app that does [describe]. Give me the full code and exact steps to run it with zero coding experience.

4. Bank Statement → Money Saved

Your statement already knows where your money goes. Claude just makes it impossible to ignore. It categorizes the month, flags every recurring subscription and obvious waste, totals what you could cut, then writes the cancellation message for each one so you actually send it. Before you paste: your own statement only, and strip account numbers, your name, and balances first. The transaction lines are all it needs.

Here's last month's transactions: [paste]. Categorize my spending, flag recurring subscriptions + waste, total what I could cut, and write the cancellation message for each.

5. Truth-Only Mode

The default failure mode of every AI is the confident guess. This kills it. Run it at the top of a chat and Claude has to say 'I'm not certain' when it is not, tell you how to verify, and flag any claim it cannot back up. It does not make the model magically right about everything, nothing does. It makes it honest about its confidence, and that is the difference between a research tool and a liability. I run it before anything where the answer actually matters.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
What you need

Ten or so photos of your own face. Different angles, different lighting, no sunglasses, no heavy filters. Front on, three quarter, and profile if you have one. The model is learning your bone structure, so give it your face from more than one side.

Then the Higgsfield plugin inside ChatGPT.

⚡ Install the Higgsfield plugin for ChatGPT

Once it's installed you never leave the chat. The plugin gives ChatGPT the image models, so the whole shoot happens in one conversation.

Step 1: Lock your face as a character

Drop all your reference photos into ChatGPT in one message, then paste this. It builds a character lock with Sol 2.0, which is the thing that keeps your face identical across every image you generate afterwards.

This is the step everyone skips, and it's the one that matters. Without a lock you get a different stranger who vaguely resembles you in every shot.

Here are reference photos of me. Using Higgsfield Sol 2.0, build a character lock from these images.

Study my face across every photo. The bone structure, the jawline, the eye shape and spacing, the hairline, the skin tone and the skin texture. Build one consistent character I can reuse in every image from now on.

Do not average my features and do not beautify them. Keep my face exactly as it is, including anything a filter would normally smooth out.

Confirm when the character is saved and tell me what to call it so I can reference it later.

Step 2: Build your look board

While the character is building, go to Pinterest and save the photos you actually want to look like. Search CEO headshot, editorial portrait, film photography portrait, or whatever fits what you're after.

Save six to ten. Pick shots that are genuinely different from each other, one clean corporate headshot, one moody side light, one outdoor golden hour, so you come out with a set instead of ten versions of the same picture.

What you are really choosing here is lighting and framing, not the person in the photo. A great reference is one where you could describe the lighting setup out loud.

Step 3: Shoot it

Drop your saved Pinterest photos into the same chat and paste this. It recreates each reference with your locked character in place of the model.

Boom. That's your headshots done, and you can keep feeding it new references forever because the character stays saved.

Here are reference photos of the look I want. Recreate each one using my locked character.

Match the reference exactly on lighting, camera angle, lens and depth of field, framing, wardrobe, colour grade and mood. The only thing that changes is the face, which is my locked character.

Shoot it as a real photograph, not a render. Keep the skin texture natural with visible pores and real shadow under the jaw. No plastic smoothing, no beauty filter, no waxy highlights.

Give me each shot at full resolution.

The things that break it

Filtered reference photos. If your selfies are already smoothed by a beauty filter, the lock learns the filter and every output looks like plastic. Use the most unedited photos you have.

One angle only. Ten front facing selfies teach it a flat face. The moment you ask for a three quarter shot it invents the side of your head. Mix the angles.

References that are all the same. Ten corporate headshots gets you ten corporate headshots. Vary the lighting on your look board and the set does the work.

Not checking the first one. Generate a single image before you run the whole board. If the face is off, the lock is off, and it's cheaper to rebuild the character than to regenerate ten images.

Frequently asked questions

Around ten, at mixed angles and in different lighting. Fewer than five and the character lock gets unreliable, especially at angles you never gave it.

You install the Higgsfield plugin into ChatGPT and work from there. Install it here , then everything happens inside your normal ChatGPT conversation.

The character lock either was not created or is not being referenced. Rebuild it with the prompt in step one, confirm ChatGPT names the character back to you, then call that name in your generation prompts.

Yes. The second prompt recreates whatever reference you feed it, so the same locked character works for editorial shots, travel photos, or fashion. Change the look board, not the prompt. Same idea as the anime version .

The giveaway is almost always over smoothed skin, which is why the prompt explicitly asks for visible pores and real shadow. If a result looks waxy, regenerate it rather than trying to fix it afterwards.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
How this works

Three pieces. A satellite screenshot of your location with a flight path drawn over it, a prompt that describes the flight shot by shot, and Higgsfield 's image-to-video generation.

The trick that makes it feel like magic: you use the annotated map as the video's start frame . The clip opens on your map, the camera dives into it, the satellite image resolves into the real world, and the drone flies the line you drew. The drawing literally comes to life.

Step 1: Draw your flight path

- Open Google Earth or Google Maps in satellite view and frame your location

- Screenshot it (portrait crop works best for 9:16)

- Draw a line over your route in any annotation tool, your phone's markup, Paint, anything. Red, thick, with a clear start and end

Routes with recognizable landmarks along the way generate dramatically better than empty terrain. Pick a path that passes 2 or 3 things the AI can name.

Step 2: The Coney Island prompt

This is the exact prompt from my video. Paste it into Higgsfield with your annotated map as the start image, 9:16, 8 to 10 seconds:

FPV drone flythrough of Coney Island, New York, 9:16 vertical, photorealistic. The video begins on the exact reference image: a top-down Google Earth satellite view of Coney Island with a red flight path line drawn across it. The camera dives INTO the map, the satellite image resolves into the real world, and the drone flies the exact route of the red line.

Shot structure: 0-1.5s the top-down map view rushes upward toward camera and dissolves into real aerial footage at the line's starting point over the Atlantic surf. 1.5-4s the drone drops to 3 meters above the waves, racing toward the beach at high speed, spray kicking up, then skims over sunbathers and umbrellas onto the sand. 4-6s it banks hard right along the Riegelmann Boardwalk, wooden planks blurring below, then rolls left around the red steel lattice of the Parachute Jump tower, structure passing within meters of the lens. 6-8s it threads between Luna Park rides, orbits the Wonder Wheel's rotating gondolas, then pulls up steeply alongside the white wooden Cyclone coaster into a rising reveal of the full shoreline, matching the map's end point.

Style: aggressive cinematic FPV, fast banking turns with camera roll, subtle speed ramps, motion blur on near objects, golden hour sunlight, sun glare flashing off the ocean, seagulls scattering, dense summer crowds, hyper-detailed, stabilized action-cam look. No text, no watermarks, no UI elements, no propellers visible.

Step 3: Generate it

In Higgsfield: image-to-video, upload your annotated map as the start image , paste the prompt, set 9:16 and 8 to 10 seconds, audio off (add sound in your edit).

Two things that will happen:

It suggests a preset instead of generating. Decline it and run your literal prompt. A preset restyles your map image, what you want is for it to animate INTO the flight.

The first render is close but not perfect. Two knobs. If the map-dive transition looks muddy, cut the first sentence of the shot structure and generate from the water-level shot instead, using the map as a plain reference. If the landmarks come out generic, make the two most famous ones more prominent in the prompt, they are what sells the location.

The meta prompt: any city on earth

You do not live at Coney Island. Give Claude your own annotated screenshot with this, and it writes the comprehensive prompt for your route:

Here is a satellite screenshot with a red flight path line drawn on it. Identify the location and the real landmarks along the route. Then write a comprehensive FPV drone video prompt for an AI video generator: 9:16 vertical, photorealistic, 8 to 10 seconds. Start the video ON this map image, dive into it, and resolve into real aerial footage that flies the exact red line. Include a timed shot structure (0-1.5s, 1.5-4s, 4-6s, 6-8s) that names the actual landmarks the line passes, concrete altitudes and banking moves, and a style block: aggressive cinematic FPV, camera roll in turns, speed ramps, motion blur, golden hour light, no text, no watermarks, no propellers visible.

Where to use this

Openers and b-roll for reels, travel content for places you have not been yet, real estate and venue flyovers, music video shots.

One honest note. This is AI footage, not aerial photography. Using it as creative is fair game, selling it to a client as a real drone survey of their property is not. Label it AI where a platform asks, and never present generated footage as documentary fact.

Frequently asked questions

You get free credits at signup, enough to test a couple of renders. Video generation runs on credits after that. Start at higgsfield.ai , the image-to-video mode is what you want.

Any place with recognizable features. Cities, coastlines, stadiums, and campuses work great. Empty fields and suburbs come out generic because the AI has nothing to anchor to. The meta prompt in this guide makes Claude name the landmarks on your specific route, which is what keeps it looking real.

Image-to-video with your annotated map as the start frame, 9:16 vertical, 8 to 10 seconds, audio off. If the tool recommends a preset, decline it and run the literal prompt.

No, that is the point. No drone, no permits, no pilot. If you want the original Google Earth Studio version of this trick, the first drone guide covers it.

As ad creative or content, yes. Do not sell it as real aerial photography or a site survey, and label it as AI-generated where the platform requires it.

Claude: pay. This is the one.

The only flat yes on this list.

I personally pay for the Max plan because I live in it all day. You almost certainly don't need that. The $20/mo plan is the one to get, and it's the only AI subscription I'd put in front of basically everyone.

The reason is simple: Claude is the best writer of the four, full stop. Scripts, captions, emails, anything where the words have to sound like a person wrote them. If only one AI charge ever hits your card, make it this one.

Perplexity: I pay, you probably shouldn't

Full honesty: I pay for Perplexity Pro at $20/mo, and I'd still tell most people to skip it.

The free version is genuinely good. It handles everyday search and research without making you feel punished for not paying, which is rare.

Upgrade only if you're doing heavy research every single day and the free tier starts getting in your way. Otherwise keep the $20 and put it toward Claude.

Gemini: free is enough

Shortest verdict on the list: the free version is enough.

Use Gemini free and keep your money. When a free tier already covers your real usage, a subscription isn't an upgrade. It's a donation.

Grok: don't pay, ever

Grok has exactly one job for me: real-time trends. When I need to know what's blowing up right now, Grok is the one that sees it. That's genuinely useful, and the free version covers it completely.

One narrow use case does not earn a monthly charge. Run your trend check, close the tab, keep your card in your wallet.

The cheat sheet

My actual stack is Claude Max plus Perplexity Pro. Those are the two I'd feel within an hour if they vanished.

Your stack, if you're starting today: one paid subscription, three free tiers, and you're not missing anything that matters. That's $20 a month instead of $80.

Pricing and tiers shift constantly, so sanity-check the numbers before you buy. The verdicts hold.

Claude: PAY. The $20/mo plan. Best writer of the four.
Gemini: FREE. The free version is enough.
Grok: FREE. Real-time trend checks only, never pay.
Perplexity: FREE for most. Pro at $20/mo only if you research all day.
Starter stack: Claude paid, the other three free. $20/mo instead of $80.

Most people don't. Start free and only upgrade when you actually hit a wall. Here is how to get every premium model free first .

What this actually does

You find an app that is already profitable, then hand its URL to an AI builder with one prompt. It studies the product, works out the one feature people actually come for, and rebuilds it as a real, working app under your own brand. Not a screenshot, the core feature genuinely functions.

Then it does the part most people miss. It wires up pricing and plans so it can make MRR, researches every competitor in the niche and builds a versus page to outrank each one, spins up hundreds of SEO blogs, and makes every result shareable so it spreads on its own.

Step 1: Find a profitable app to copy

Open TrustMRR and sort the list by revenue, high to low. You are looking for a product that is already making money and is easy to rebuild: one clear core feature, not a sprawling platform.

In the video I picked a face-scoring app doing around $16K a month. Copy the URL of whatever profitable app you land on, you will drop it into the prompt next.

https://trustmrr.com/acquire

Step 2: Open Emergent

Emergent is the AI builder doing all the heavy lifting here. It crawls the target, builds the real working product, wires the payments and auth, and deploys it live, all from one prompt. Start a project, then paste the prompt below into it.

https://app.emergent.sh/?utm_shift=redirect&via=ariacodez

Step 3: Paste this one prompt

Drop your target app's URL into the prompt where it says [PASTE THE TARGET URL HERE], then paste the whole thing into Emergent.

The trick is in the defaults. Every setup choice is already decided for you, so Emergent never stops to interrogate you, it just builds and ships.

Build me a complete, production-ready SaaS: the ACTUAL WORKING PRODUCT at [PASTE THE TARGET URL HERE], rebuilt as my own brand and genuinely BETTER. Not a marketing clone, the real functional tool, with accounts, a pricing and payments system, a full marketing site, SEO, viral sharing, and polished design, deployed live and ready to make MRR.

DECIDE EVERYTHING YOURSELF. DO NOT STOP TO ASK ME. Assume all of these defaults and just build:
- Brand: invent a strong, memorable brand name and one-line tagline that fit the niche. If I paste my own at the very end, use mine instead.
- Stack: Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind, a real database (use whatever this environment gives you, MongoDB is fine), server-rendered for SEO, deployed live with a public URL.
- AI engine: use the built-in universal LLM key in this environment, no key from me. For the core analysis pick the fastest, cheapest, capable vision model yourself (Gemini Flash or similar).
- Auth: use the platform's managed sign-in (Google + email). Do not make me set up any cloud console.
- Payments: build the FULL pricing, upgrade flow, usage limits, and billing portal, but run Stripe in test mode. Do NOT ask me for keys, wire it so I drop live keys in later and it goes live.
- Generate real finished content. No lorem ipsum, no placeholders, no "coming soon", no fake features. It works on first use.

STEP 1, STUDY THE TARGET. Crawl the URL and work out exactly what it does: core function, exact inputs and outputs, every feature, pricing, and limits. This is my own better version.

STEP 2, BUILD THE REAL WORKING PRODUCT. Build the actual tool end to end: real inputs, real AI processing, real outputs. Real accounts, a dashboard, and saved history of past results.

STEP 3, MONETIZE IT. A genuinely useful free tier, then monthly and annual paid plans: clean upgrade flow, limits on free, unlocked volume on paid, billing portal to manage and cancel. Ready to take real recurring payments the moment I add keys.

Pages (static, commercial intent, in the nav): Home with the live product front and center, Features, Pricing with its own FAQ, use-case pages, About, Contact, plus programmatic landing pages for high-intent long-tail. Blog (informational, dated, categorized): a pillar and cluster model, seed 12+ real 800 to 1500 word posts, each with one H1, a TL;DR, internal links to the money pages, an author byline, and a CTA into the product.

STEP 5, OUTRANK EVERY COMPETITOR (the weapon). Research the market and find the REAL, named top 8 to 12 competitors and alternatives in this exact category. Do not invent them, search them out. For EACH one, build a dedicated versus page at /vs/[competitor]: an honest side by side ("where they are strong" and "where I win"), a feature and pricing table, an FAQ, and a clear CTA, written to rank for "[competitor] alternative" and "[my brand] vs [competitor]". Add category pages: "best [category] tool", "best [competitor] alternative", and "[product] for [use case]". Then generate a large comparison-driven blog cluster, hundreds of posts at scale, every long-tail question in the niche, each one internally linked to the versus pages and the money pages. Full technical SEO on everything: per-page title, meta, canonical, Open Graph and Twitter cards, a per-page OG image, JSON-LD (Organization, WebSite, SoftwareApplication, Article, BreadcrumbList, FAQPage, Product and Offer), an FAQ block on every key page, internal linking everywhere, auto sitemap.xml and robots.txt, clean slugs. Target 95+ Lighthouse on Performance and SEO.

STEP 6, MAKE IT GO VIRAL. Every result is one-tap shareable via the Web Share API with desktop fallbacks (X, Facebook, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Reddit, copy link, download image). Every result gets a permanent, indexable /r/[id] page, branded, with a "make your own" CTA, that is the viral loop and it ranks. Auto-generate a dynamic OG image per result so shares unfurl as a clean branded card. If the niche fits, add a public leaderboard or battle so people share to climb it.

STEP 7, DESIGN. One bold, cohesive aesthetic that fits the niche, never default purple-on-white slop. A real design system: CSS-variable color tokens, a type scale pairing a distinctive display font with a clean body font, 8pt spacing, consistent radius and shadow. A real hero with the working product usable immediately, a social-proof strip, alternating feature sections, scannable pricing, a full footer, tasteful motion, and flawless mobile-first responsive.

STEP 8, SHIP. Deploy it live and give me the URL. Confirm the product works, sign-up works, and the test-mode payment flow works end to end. Then hand me a punch list of what to expand, and the top 10 keywords each money page and versus page targets.

Build the whole thing end to end, the working product first, then everything around it. Do not pause between steps. Ship a complete, working, monetizable, SEO-loaded, beautifully designed SaaS I could launch and charge for today.

Why it's one prompt, not ten

Most people get this method half-working because the builder keeps stopping to ask: what's the brand, which AI model, what are your Stripe keys, which auth, which database. Every question is a chance for the build to stall.

This prompt answers all of them up front. It tells Emergent to name the brand itself, use the built-in AI key, run payments in test mode (so you never hand over keys), use managed Google and email sign-in, and use whatever database is there. So it builds the working product first, then the marketing site, the SEO, and the viral loop around it, without pausing once.

The weapon: outrank every competitor

This is the part that compounds. The prompt makes Emergent research the real, named competitors in your niche, then build a dedicated versus page for each one.

For a face-scoring app that means honest side-by-side pages against the likes of Umax, LooksMax AI, Mogged, Qoves, and the original you copied, each one tuned to rank for "[competitor] alternative" and "vs [competitor]". On top of that it spins up a large blog cluster on every long-tail question in the niche, all interlinked.

Comparison and alternative searches are the highest-intent traffic on the internet. Someone typing "best [tool] alternative" is ready to switch. You build the page that answers that exact search and you catch them at the moment they are looking.

How it goes viral

Every result a user generates is one-tap shareable, and gets its own permanent, indexable page with a "make your own" button and a clean branded preview image. If the niche fits, it adds a public leaderboard or battle so people share to climb it.

That is the loop: every user who shares a result creates a new page that ranks and pulls in the next user, for free.

One rule

Use this to build your own product, not to pass off someone else's brand as yours. Rebuild the idea and the functionality, never the name, logo, copy, or trademarks. Keep every comparison honest, lopsided fake ones get filtered by Google and burn trust, win on what you genuinely do better. If your app gives financial, medical, or legal output, label it as educational and not professional advice.

Frequently asked questions

Use TrustMRR to see which apps are actually making money, sort by revenue, and pick a profitable one with a clear core feature that is easy to rebuild.

It decides every setup choice for you, brand, AI model, payments in test mode, auth, and database, so the builder never stops to ask and just ships. Then it builds the versus pages and blogs to outrank the original.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
Why this matters

Data brokers and people-search sites scrape and sell your personal info to anyone who looks you up. Your home address, your phone number, even your family members are sitting on dozens of these sites right now, and you never signed up for any of it.

The good news: it is your data, and you have the legal right to remove it for free. These companies will try to charge you 100 to 300 dollars a year to do it. You do not need them. ChatGPT can find every site and handle the removals for you.

What you'll need

ChatGPT (the free version is enough to find the sites and write every removal request). Your full name, your current and past cities, and your phone number. About 5 minutes.

One honest note: the auto-submit step uses Agent Mode, which is on ChatGPT's paid plan. If you are on free, do not worry. ChatGPT still hands you every opt-out link and a ready-to-send removal request, so you just paste and submit them yourself. Same result, a few extra minutes.

Step 1 - Find every site exposing you

Open a new ChatGPT chat and paste this. It pulls up every data broker and people-search site showing your info, with the exact opt-out link for each.

Act as a privacy expert. List every data broker and people-search site showing my name, address, and phone, with the exact opt-out link for each.

Step 2 - Get your removal requests written

Now have it write the actual takedown requests for you, plus how to clear yourself out of Google search results.

Write the exact removal request to send each one, and show me how to pull my info off Google too.

Step 3 - Let it submit them (Agent Mode)

Turn on Agent Mode (hit the + in the chat box and toggle it on), then send this. It goes site to site and submits each removal for you. On the free plan, just open the opt-out links from Step 1 and paste in the requests from Step 2 yourself.

Go to every one of those sites and submit the removal for me.

Step 4 - Stay gone (weekly auto-recheck)

Sites love to quietly re-add you. This makes ChatGPT set up a weekly task that re-checks and re-submits until you are completely gone.

Now re-check every week and re-submit any site that ignores it until I'm gone.

Stay safe

This only removes your own data, which is completely within your rights. Never pay a finder or removal service, the prompts above do the same thing for free. Removals are not instant, most sites take a few days to a few weeks to drop you, so let the weekly task keep working. Be safe out there. 🤯

Frequently asked questions

ChatGPT finds the data-broker sites holding your address, phone and family, then runs the removal chain that wipes you off, for free.

Yes, the chain uses the brokers' own opt-out forms. The manual checklist version is here .

The finding is minutes. Removals take days to weeks to clear, and some need a re-check.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
Before you start, read this

This is a brand new beta and it is powerful. A few rules that keep you out of trouble:

Use a separate sandbox account. Robinhood lets you open a dedicated agentic account, fund only that, and the agent can never touch your main portfolio.

Start small. Only deposit what you are genuinely fine losing while you learn how it behaves.

Keep approvals on. You can make the agent ask permission before every trade. Do that while you are learning, even though you can flip everything to always allow.

This is not financial advice. The AI can be wrong, act on outdated information, and Robinhood's own warning says these agents can move too fast to stop in real time. You are responsible for every trade it places.

Step 1 - Get access to the Robinhood agentic beta

Open the link below on a computer, opt into the agentic trading beta, and open your dedicated agentic account. Heads up: Robinhood only lets you set this up and approve the agent on a desktop, not the phone app.

robinhood.com/agent

Step 2 - Connect Claude to your Robinhood

You only need one link for this, and the exact same link works on every version of Claude . Copy it now, you will paste it in a second:

https://agent.robinhood.com/mcp/trading

Step 2a - Claude Desktop or Cowork (easiest, no code)

The simple point and click way. In the Claude desktop app, or in Cowork, on a computer:

- Click Settings.

- Open the Connectors tab.

- Click Add custom connector.

- Name it Robinhood.

- In the link or URL box, paste the link from above: https://agent.robinhood.com/mcp/trading

- Click Add, then Connect.

- A Robinhood window pops up. Log in and approve access.

That is it, Claude is connected. If you do not see a Connectors tab, update Claude to the latest version first.

Step 2b - Claude Code (only if you use the terminal)

Prefer the terminal? Skip the menus. Paste this one line, then type /mcp inside Claude Code , pick robinhood-trading from the list, and approve the login:

claude mcp add robinhood-trading --transport http https://agent.robinhood.com/mcp/trading

Step 3 - Create and fund the agentic account

Once connected, Robinhood creates a dedicated agentic trading account, completely separate from your normal portfolio. Fund it with an amount you are comfortable losing. Start small. This is the only money your agent can ever access, so it is your hard safety limit.

Step 4 - Set the agent's permissions

Your agent now has hundreds of tools to read your account, research the market, and place trades. Robinhood lets you moderate it: you can require approval before specific actions, or set tools to always allow. The recommendation while you are learning is to keep trades on Needs Approval, so nothing happens without your tap. You can loosen it later once you trust it.

Step 5 - Build your watchlist with deep research

This is the first prompt from the video. Claude will ask you a couple of questions about your risk tolerance and how many names you want, then it spins up multiple research agents in parallel to dig through the sector and build a watchlist to your criteria. Paste this:

Do deep research on undervalued stocks related to semiconductors and AI then create a watchlist of the best ones using the Robinhood connector.

Step 6 - Set the scheduled trading task

This is the second prompt. It turns Claude into a scheduled task that runs on its own. Every market open it checks your watchlist, looks for an entry, and asks your permission before it places anything. You stay in control of every trade. Paste this:

Act as a professional hedge fund trading specialist. Create a scheduled task that checks this watchlist every market open and notifies me if there is a good trade entry and ask my permission to place the trade.

Stay safe

Quick recap of the guardrails:

Sandbox account only, never your main one. Start with a small amount. Keep trades on Needs Approval while you learn.

It is not financial advice and the AI can be wrong. Robinhood warns these agents can move too fast to stop and can act on bad information.

You can disconnect the agent instantly at any time, and you get a notification on every action it takes. Use those.

Claude is a beast, here is what else you can have it do

Once it is connected, the watchlist and the scheduled task are just the start. Tap to copy any of these into the same chat:

Risk x-ray

Analyze my whole account for risk and concentration and tell me what is overexposed.

Morning brief

Every morning before open, brief me on my watchlist, the overnight news, and what is moving.

Earnings radar

Alert me the moment any name on my watchlist reports earnings or gets an analyst upgrade or downgrade.

Unusual activity watch

Watch for unusual volume or options activity on my watchlist and ping me.

Social sentiment

Compare my watchlist to what is trending on X and Reddit and flag anything with building hype.

Weekly refresh

Every Sunday, re-run the research and tell me if a new name belongs on the list.

End of day recap

After close, recap what moved today and why in one short message.

Position-size guardrail

Never let any single position be more than 10 percent of the account, and tell me if it drifts past that.

Explain like I am five

Before I buy anything, explain the company and the risk to me in plain English.

One last thing

This is brand new and genuinely powerful. Start in the sandbox, keep approvals on, and never risk what you cannot lose. Be safe out there.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
What this actually does

You give an AI app builder the URL of a live website. It studies the site, works out what the product is and the one feature that makes it special, then rebuilds it as a real, working app. Not a screenshot. The core feature actually functions.

Then you bolt on a set of comparison pages so your version starts showing up for the original app's traffic. People searching for that app, or for alternatives to it, land on yours instead.

What you need

Blink, the AI app builder that does the heavy lifting. You start a free account in Step 1.

The URL of an app you want to rebuild. Pick one with a real, feature-rich product. A dashboard, a marketplace, an AI tool. Not a plain blog. The more the app actually does, the more impressive the rebuild.

That is it. About two minutes of setup.

Step 1: Open Blink

Blink is the AI app builder doing all the work here. Start a free account, then open a new project and paste the prompt below into it.

https://blink.new/?via=ariacodez

Step 2: Rebuild the app

Drop your target app's URL into the prompt where it says so, then paste the whole thing into Blink. It probes the site and builds a real, working version. Design matched, and the main feature fully functional, not a dead mockup.

You are a senior full-stack engineer and product designer. I'm going to give
you the URL of a live website. Probe it, understand exactly what it does, then
rebuild it as a real, fully working web app. Not a static mockup, the real thing.

Reference site: [paste the URL here]

PHASE 1: Probe and understand it
Open the URL and study it properly before writing any code. Work out:
- What the product actually is: its core promise, the problem it solves, and who it is for.
- The one core feature that makes it special, the thing people actually come here to do. Getting this right matters more than anything else.
- Every page, and how the navigation connects them.
- The full visual design: exact color palette, fonts, headline sizes, spacing, layout, buttons, cards, icons, background, and overall vibe.
- The copy and its tone.
- The data and state involved: inputs, uploads, results, accounts, history.

PHASE 2: Rebuild it for real

Make the core feature actually work
- Build the main feature end to end so it genuinely functions. If it is AI powered, for example it analyzes an uploaded image or photo, answers a question, generates something, or gives a recommendation, wire it to a real AI model so it truly takes the user's input, processes it, and returns a real result. Do not fake it with a hardcoded answer.
- Present the result in a clean, well designed layout that fits the product: cards, labels, scores, color coding, a clear verdict.
- If the product gives financial, medical, or legal output, add a short "for educational purposes only, not professional advice" line in the UI, the way the real tools do.

Match the design
- Recreate the look closely: same colors, same typography feel, same layout, same spacing, same component styles, same energy. It should feel like the same brand.
- Fully responsive, flawless on mobile and desktop.
- Finished and polished: hover states, smooth transitions, loading states, empty states, sensible defaults.

Build the whole flow
- Recreate the supporting pages too: the landing page, sign up or sign in, and wherever the core feature lives.
- Seed everything with realistic sample data so no screen ever looks empty.
- Where the original feels dated or clunky, improve it, but keep the same product identity.
- If anything is unclear, make a smart product decision and keep going. Never stop to ask, just build the most sensible version.

When you are done, give me a working app I can click through end to end, with the core feature fully functional, plus a short summary of what you built and how the main flow works.

Step 3: Outrank the original

Once the app is built, send this as a follow up in the same chat. It researches the real competitors, then builds a set of comparison pages tuned to rank on Google and funnel that search traffic straight into your app.

Now that the app is built, add a full set of comparison pages to it so it can rank on Google
and pull in search traffic. Keep the exact same design, brand, and components as the app you
just built, these pages are part of the same site.

Research first
- Take the original brand at the URL I gave you, and research the market to find 5 to 8 real
  competing or alternative products in the same category. Pick the closest and most searched ones.

Then build
- A comparison hub page at /compare that lists every comparison with a short blurb and a link.
- One comparison page per competitor at a clean slug like /compare/[competitor-name].
- Plus one page comparing this app against that original brand at the URL.

Make every comparison page rank
- A keyword targeted page title and H1, for example "[This app] vs [Competitor]: features, pricing and which is better in 2026".
- A unique meta description and Open Graph tags.
- A clear side by side comparison table: key features, pricing, free option, speed, accuracy, ease of use, and pros and cons for each.
- A short honest intro and a clear verdict. Favor this app where it genuinely wins, but stay fair and accurate. Do not invent fake weaknesses, dishonest comparisons get penalized by Google and kill trust.
- An FAQ section answering what people actually type into search, for example "Is [this app] a good [Competitor] alternative?" and "[Competitor] vs [this app], which is better?".
- Structured data markup (Product, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList) so the pages can show rich results.
- A clear call to action on every page that sends the reader to sign up and try the core feature.
- Internal links from the landing page to the hub, and between the comparison pages.

Target the searches people actually make: "[brand] alternative", "[brand] vs [competitor]",
"best [category] tool", and "[competitor] alternatives".

Also tidy up SEO across the whole site while you are at it: semantic HTML, fast load, a descriptive
title and meta description on every page, a sitemap, and clean readable URLs.

When you are done, show me the comparison hub and tell me which competitors you chose and why.

Why it works

Two things make this hit.

First, the prompt forces the AI to make the core feature genuinely work with real AI under the hood, instead of faking a pretty mockup. That is the difference between a demo and a product.

Second, comparison and alternative pages are some of the highest intent traffic on the internet. Someone typing "best [tool] alternative" is ready to switch. Build the page that answers that exact search and you catch them at the moment they are looking.

Get the best results

Pick a feature-rich app. The bigger the product, the bigger the wow.

Give your app a name when it asks, so the comparison pages read cleanly.

Keep every comparison honest. Lopsided fake ones get filtered by Google and burn trust. Win on the things you genuinely do better.

When you are happy with it, deploy it and put it on a real domain so the SEO actually compounds over time.

One rule

Use this to learn, and to build your own product. Not to pass off someone else's brand as yours. Do not copy a company's name, logo, or content word for word. Rebuild the idea, make it your own, and keep your comparisons truthful. If your app gives financial, medical, or legal output, label it as educational and not professional advice.

Frequently asked questions

Give it a URL and it rebuilds the app as your own, then builds the pages to outrank the original on Google. Claude Code does the heavy lifting.

No. You describe and direct, the AI writes and ships. Here are the coding tools I actually use .

Rebuild the functionality, not the brand, copy, or trademarks. This is about building your own version, not ripping one off.

The play

You are not inventing anything. You find an app that is ALREADY making money, clone it (legally, your own code and brand) with AI, make it cleaner, and sell the finished product to someone who would rather buy than build.

Three steps: find it on TrustMRR, build it on Blink, flip it on Acquire or Flippa.

Step 1: Find a money-making app (TrustMRR)

Go to TrustMRR . It lists real startups and apps with their actual monthly revenue. Sort by revenue high to low , then find a SIMPLE one.

Example: an app whose whole job is to analyze what colors suit you, already making solid recurring revenue. Simple feature, proven demand. Copy the app's description , you will paste it into the build prompt next.

How to pick the right one

What makes an app worth cloning (look for all of these on TrustMRR):

- ONE simple core feature you can describe in a sentence.

- Already making recurring revenue (the higher the MRR, the more proven the demand).

- Weak or dated design you can easily beat.

- A broad audience, not a tiny niche. Sort by revenue high to low and pick the simplest one near the top.

Step 2: Clone it with Blink

Go to Blink , use my link for $10 in free credits to start. Paste the prompt below and replace the bracketed description with the description you copied from TrustMRR.

Build a production-ready full-stack web app. Here is exactly what it does:

[PASTE THE PRODUCT DESCRIPTION you copied from TrustMRR here]

Build all of this:
- A clean, modern landing page with the core tool front and center, better designed than a typical competitor.
- The main feature working end to end.
- Email and password auth, plus a backend database that saves each user and their results.
- A pricing page with a free tier and two paid tiers, with Stripe checkout fully wired up.
- Programmatic SEO pages: auto-generate "compare" and "[my app] vs [competitor]" pages and "best [category] tools" pages so it ranks on Google.
- Fully mobile responsive, fast, and deployable as is.

Make it cleaner and more polished than the original. Deliver it working in a single shot.

Step 3: What the prompt builds

Within minutes you get the exact app, fully functional and usually cleaner than the original. The prompt is built to include everything a buyer wants to see:

- a working product with auth and a real backend database

- pricing tiers with Stripe checkout already wired up

- programmatic SEO compare pages that rank you on Google for free traffic

That combination is what turns a clone into something sellable, not just a demo.

Step 4: Flip it

Now you sell it. List it on Acquire.com or Flippa , the two big marketplaces for buying and selling online businesses. People pay good money for ready-made, working apps because it saves them months of building.

The more it shows (a clean product, some traffic from the SEO pages, a Stripe account ready to go), the more it is worth.

Bonus: make it more sellable

A few things that raise the value before you list:

- Get a handful of real users even if free, traction sells.

- Publish the compare/SEO pages so a buyer sees Google traffic potential.

- Connect Stripe and leave it ready, buyers love a turnkey checkout.

- Write a one-page summary : what it does, the idea behind it, and the room to grow.

Frequently asked questions

You are building your own version of a proven idea with your own code (via AI), your own brand, and your own design, which is how most software businesses start. Do not copy their exact name, logo, or any copyrighted content, build your own better version of the same concept.

No. Blink writes and runs all the code from your prompt. TrustMRR is just a list you browse, and Acquire/Flippa are listing sites.

Blink has a free tier and my link gives you $10 in credits to start, TrustMRR has free browsing, and listing on Acquire or Flippa is free. You can do the whole chain without paying upfront.

It varies with the app's revenue and traffic, the more proven and polished it is, the more it is worth. Even one with no revenue yet has value because it saves the buyer the build time.

One simple core feature, already making recurring money, a broad audience, and a weak design you can easily beat. Sort TrustMRR by revenue and pick the simplest one near the top.

What this actually does

AI detectors flag patterns: inflated word choice, identical sentence lengths, robotic transitions, endless hedging. This makes ChatGPT learn those exact patterns from the source, then permanently avoid them. You set it once in Custom Instructions and it applies to every new chat automatically.

Step 1: Make ChatGPT learn the tells

Open a new chat and paste this. It sends ChatGPT to Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing page, the actual list of patterns that expose AI text.

Step 2: Turn the tells into one permanent rule

Right after it answers, paste this. It compresses everything into a single instruction you can save.

Now turn every one of those tells into a hard rule you must never break. Then compress all of them into ONE permanent instruction, written as direct commands to yourself, that makes everything you write from now on sound naturally human: vary sentence length, use plain words over inflated ones, cut filler transitions, stop over-hedging, no cliches, real specifics over vague summaries. Output only that final instruction, ready to paste, under 1500 characters.

Step 3: Save it to memory (this is what makes it permanent)

Copy the instruction ChatGPT just gave you, then:

- Open ChatGPT and go to Settings > Personalization .

- Set your tone to Efficient , it cuts the fluff at the source.

- Open Custom Instructions , and in the box for how ChatGPT should respond, paste the instruction.

- Save.

It is now applied to every new chat automatically. You never paste it again.

Step 4: Test it

Drop in something ChatGPT wrote for you before and have it rewrite under the new rules. Run the result through any AI detector to check.

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
Paste this into any AI chatbot

⚡ Open Higgsfield

Works with Claude , ChatGPT , or any capable chatbot. Swap the last line for your actual recipe, send it, then paste the one prompt it gives you into Higgsfield to generate it.

ANIME COOKING MONTAGE — PROMPT GENERATOR BRIEF
You generate Seedance video prompts for 15-second anime-style cooking montages. I'll give you a recipe. You return one prompt, not commentary on the recipe.
Fixed style block — appears in the prompt, unchanged:
Modern anime cel-shaded style, crisp black line art, painterly gradients, bright naturalistic kitchen daylight, soft bloom, shallow depth of field, subtle film grain, no text, no subtitles, no watermark.
Fixed setting — sunlit stainless-steel kitchen, vertical 9:16, a man's hands with a silver band ring on one finger, rapid macro cuts. The character (when seen) is a tall dark-haired man in a black sleeveless top. Generate one character reference image of him first and reuse it for every recipe, so he's the same person video after video.
Fixed structure — 13 beats over 15 seconds, in this shape:
Beats 1-4, 0.0-4.3s: Prep. Macro on hands. Fast cuts, 0.9-1.3s each.
Beat 5, 4.3-5.2s: Static beat before the transformation. No hands in frame.
Beats 6-7, 5.2-7.7s: The transformation. Slow motion, high-speed camera detail. Longest combined block.
Beat 8, 7.7-8.8s: Extraction / reveal of the finished element.
Beat 9, 8.8-10.5s: Wide static shot with the character. Locked camera, minimal movement, he blinks.
Beat 10, 10.5-11.6s: Close-up payoff on the finished item, backlit.
Beats 11-12, 11.6-13.5s: Sauce / garnish / accompaniment.
Beat 13, 13.5-15.0s: Final plated hero shot. Very slow push-in, steam, light glint.
Your job when I give a recipe
Identify the money shot — the single most visually dramatic moment (sear, splash, emulsion toss, batter ribbon, cheese pull, flame). It gets beats 6-7 and the slow motion.
Pick the 3-4 most visually distinct prep steps for beats 1-4. Drop the rest. Skip anything invisible ("season to taste").
Flag it upfront if the dish is a poor fit — anything cooked covered or in an oven has no visible transformation, so beats 6-7 become a lid-lift reveal instead. Say so before writing.
Write physically, not procedurally. Describe motion, weight, and material behavior: things fall freely and tumble, they don't descend vertically; liquids ripple outward and settle; foam radiates in sheets and thins. Never write an object as rigid or rail-guided — that's the main failure mode.
Deliver one prompt: the combined 15s prompt, style block then timestamped beats in the format 0.0-0.9s — [description]. Keep it under 5,000 characters.
Settings to state at the end: 9:16. Both Seedance 2.5 and Seedance 2.0 are unlimited right now, use whichever fits: Seedance 2.0 is 1080p and generates the full 15 seconds natively in one pass, no splitting needed. Seedance 2.5 is 720p with more runway per generation. If you land on a tier that caps shorter than 15s, split the prompt at the 7.7s mark into two clips instead.
Known failure modes to preempt in your output: the transformation reads limp if described with force words ("violent," "explosive") instead of shape words ("crown-shaped," "radiating sheets," "wings"); image-to-video anchors hard to the reference pose, so ease into any falling or tumbling motion rather than starting on it; beats 6-7 are one continuous event split across a cut, so lock the seed across both.
My recipe:
"PASTE YOUR RECIPE HERE"

No. Paste this into Claude , ChatGPT , or similar, it writes one prompt. Paste that into Higgsfield to generate the video.

No. Anything cooked covered or in an oven has no visible transformation moment, so the prompt flags it and swaps in a lid-lift reveal instead.

Why faceless kids cartoons

Animated kids channels pull hundreds of thousands of views per video, and YouTube pays roughly $200 to $3,000 per 100,000 views . You never show your face and you never animate by hand. One repeating character plus a daily upload is a channel that compounds. The whole point of this setup is to make the daily upload take minutes, then almost no time at all.

Step 1: Connect Higgsfield to Claude

This wires Higgsfield's video engine straight into Claude through the MCP. Two minutes, no code.

1. Open Claude (claude.ai) -> Settings -> Connectors -> Add custom connector
2. Go to higgsfield.ai/mcp and copy the MCP link
3. Paste it in, name it Higgsfield, save
4. Use the Seedance 2.0 model for the cartoon look

Step 2: Add the AI Kids Cartoon Videos skill

This is the custom skill that tells Claude exactly how to build a video that holds a toddler's attention: the look, the song structure, character consistency, and the scene formula. Grab it free here: the AI Kids Cartoon Videos skill . Open SKILL.md , then upload it as a skill in Claude (or paste it into a Project).

github.com/AKCodez/ai-kids-cartoon-videos

Step 3: Generate your first video

Now you just ask. Claude plans the character, writes the song, and drives Higgsfield to render every scene, in under a minute.

Using the AI Kids Cartoon Videos skill and Higgsfield, generate one original, wholesome kids cartoon video: pick a character and a micro-lesson, write a short sing-along song, then generate every scene. Keep one character consistent the whole way through.

Step 4: Predict virality, post only the winners

Do not post everything. Generate a batch, score them, post only the best. This is the virality score tool : it rates each video on the things that actually drive a kids video, and you only upload the top scorers.

Score this video 0-100 for a kids audience on: hook strength (first 2 seconds), watch-through, and rewatch + shareability. Give me the number and one specific fix. Only the highest scorers get posted.

Step 5: Put it on autopilot with a scheduled task

This is where it runs while you sleep. Ask Claude to create a scheduled task that does the whole loop every morning: generate the prompts with the skill, render them through Higgsfield, score them, and surface the winners ready to post. You wake up to finished videos.

Create a scheduled task that runs every day at 6am: use the /ai-kids-cartoon-videos skill to generate prompts for 10 original videos, then bring each one to life with the Higgsfield MCP. Once they are rendered, run the virality score tool on all 10, rank them, and surface the best ones ready for me to post. Keep every video original and wholesome.

Step 6: Post daily and get paid

Upload your best video each day, set it to Made for Kids (required), and group videos into playlists by theme so autoplay keeps the watch-time rolling. Post the same character every day so it becomes a real show. Once the channel is monetized, the back catalog earns while you keep shipping. source_metadata.title: Delete Everything Google Knows About You (The A to Z Guide)
source_metadata.access_status: Public page fetched successfully; visible article content available

content_payload.full_walkthrough_raw:
Read this first

Turning a setting off only stops new data from being saved. It does not remove what is already stored.

Deleting is a separate step and almost every guide online skips it. It is Part 3 below. If you only do the toggles, years of history stay exactly where it is.

Part 1: See what they already have

Start here. The settings mean a lot more once you have seen the file.

Your activity log. myactivity.google.com is every search, every app you opened, every video you watched, with timestamps. Scroll to the bottom to see how far back it goes.

Your ad profile. myadcenter.google.com is the profile advertisers buy against. It lists the age range, relationship status, income bracket and interests that were guessed about you.

Your voice recordings. myactivity.google.com/product/assistant holds real audio clips if voice activity was ever switched on. They play right in the browser.

Everything, in one export. takeout.google.com exports the lot. Press Select all and you will see it covers 61 separate products. The finished archive is often tens of gigabytes.

Which products hold data on you. myaccount.google.com/dashboard is the service by service breakdown.

Part 2: The master switch page

Almost every toggle lives on one page. Open it and work down the list.

Web and App Activity. The big one. It records searches, app usage, and location alongside them. When you turn it off, also uncheck the two subsettings, because they are separate boxes and they do not switch off with the parent:

- Include Chrome history and activity from sites, apps and devices that use Google services

- Include voice and audio activity

YouTube History. Records what you watch and what you search on YouTube. Uncheck its three subsettings too: the videos you watch, your searches, and YouTube voice and audio activity.

Personalized Recommendations in Search services. Uses your account data to shape what Search shows you.

Play Personalization. The same idea for the Play Store.

Personalized ads. Opens My Ad Center. Switch ad personalization off there.

Partner ad settings. A separate control on the same panel, covering ads on non Google sites and apps that partner with Google. Most people miss this one because it sits under the ads section instead of with the activity toggles.

https://myactivity.google.com/activitycontrols

Part 3: Delete what is already stored

Switching off stops the recording. This step clears the tape.

On each activity control, open Manage activity , then Delete , then All time . Do it for Web and App Activity, for YouTube History, and for voice and audio activity.

Then set an auto delete window so it never builds back up. Every control has a Choose an auto delete option link. Pick 3 months, which is the shortest Google offers.

Two more places worth clearing while you are in there:

Purchases and orders. myactivity.google.com/purchases pulls receipts out of Gmail into a shopping history you never asked for.

Results about you. myactivity.google.com/results-about-you finds your phone number, home address and email inside Google Search results and lets you request removal. This one is not about ads. It is about strangers finding you.

Part 4: The settings that live somewhere else

This is where most guides stop, and where the real exposure is.

Location. Location History is now called Timeline and it moved onto your phone. Open the Google Maps app, tap your profile picture, then Your Timeline. Turn it off there and delete the history. Apps that can read your account. myaccount.google.com/connections lists every third party app you ever signed into with Google, and exactly what each one can see. Apps you forgot about years ago still have access. Remove anything you do not actively use.

Devices signed into your account. myaccount.google.com/device-activity shows every device with a live session. Sign out anything you do not recognise or no longer own.

Third party cookies in Chrome. Open Chrome settings, then Privacy and security, then Third party cookies, and choose Block. These are still on by default, so nothing changes unless you change it yourself.

Chrome ad topics. In the same Privacy and security menu, open the ad privacy section and turn off what is listed there.

Gmail smart features. In Gmail , go to Settings, then See all settings, then General, and turn off smart features and personalization. This is the setting that reads message content to power suggestions.

Your advertising ID on the phone. On Android: Settings, then Privacy, then Ads, then delete the advertising ID. On iPhone: Settings, then Privacy and Security, then Tracking, then turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track.

One last thing
